Overview of Class 3

At the end of this class you can

  • define vulnerability, threat, threat actor, cyberattack, attack vector and attack surface;
  • tell apart eight common types of cyberattack and name the property of the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad that each one harms;
  • state, for each attack type, what a monitoring tool can observe and in which data source;
  • explain prevention, detection and response, and give examples of controls for each function;
  • explain why prevention alone is never sufficient, and what detection needs in order to work;
  • read a short logon log, recognize two password attacks in it and write the result as an incident note.

Opening

Slide 1

Common Types of Cyberattacks and Basic Cyber Defense Concepts

Slide 2

Today: two questions, six objectives

Welcome to Class 3 of Preventative Monitoring. Yesterday, in Class 2, we defined cybersecurity and the three properties that it protects. Today we complete the foundations with two questions. First: in what ways can these properties be attacked? Second: what can an organization do about it, before, during and after an attack?

Slide 3

Recap of Class 2: the three properties

A short recap of Class 2. Confidentiality means that information is read only by the people who are authorized to read it. Integrity means that information is complete, and is changed only by authorized people in authorized ways. Availability means that information and systems can be used when they are needed. Together, these three properties form the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad. Every attack that we study today harms at least one of them, and I will name the property each time.

Slide 4

Why a monitoring technician studies attack types

Why does a monitoring technician study attack types? Because a monitoring tool never displays the word attack. It displays events: a failed logon, a new process, a connection to an unknown address, a sudden rise in traffic. Your work is to recognize which attack can produce these events. A technician who knows the attack types knows what to look for, and where to look. This is performance criterion 1.2 of the competency of this course: precise differentiation between various types of cyberattacks. Lesson 1.4 covers criterion 1.3: appropriate illustration of cyber defense concepts.

Reading

Slide 6

Lesson 1.3 Common types of cyberattacks

Six terms to use with precision

Slide 7

Six terms to use with precision (1/2)

We start with six terms. You will meet them in every document of this program, so learn the exact wording. A vulnerability is a weakness in a system, in a configuration or in a human procedure that can be used to cause harm. Examples: a missing security update, a password that is easy to guess, an employee who was never trained to verify the sender of a message. A threat is any circumstance or event that can cause harm by using a vulnerability. A threat actor is the person or the group behind a threat: a criminal group, a dishonest employee, a state organization, or a person with little skill who runs tools written by others.

Slide 8

Six terms to use with precision (2/2)

A cyberattack is a deliberate action by a threat actor against the confidentiality, the integrity or the availability of information or systems. The word deliberate matters: a disk failure harms availability, but it is an accident, not an attack. An attack vector is the path used to reach the target: an e-mail message, a web form, a remote logon service, a USB (Universal Serial Bus) key, a stolen laptop. The attack surface is the total of all the points where an attacker can try to enter. Each new service that can be reached from the Internet enlarges the attack surface, and therefore the list of things that you must monitor.

Reference for these terms: An introduction to the cyber threat environment , published by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security .

Eight types of cyberattack, and what monitoring can observe

Slide 9

Attack type 1: Reconnaissance

Attack type 1: reconnaissance. Before attacking, a threat actor collects information about the target: which addresses answer, which services are open, which software versions are used, which employees are named on the public website. The technical form is network scanning: a program sends connection requests to many addresses and many ports, and records the answers. Reconnaissance harms nothing directly, so many lists of attacks leave it out. For us it is the earliest warning sign. What monitoring can observe: in the firewall log, one external source that tries many ports or many addresses within a few seconds.

Slide 10

Attack type 2: Social engineering and phishing

Attack type 2: social engineering, and its most frequent form, phishing. Social engineering is the manipulation of a person, so that this person gives information or performs an action that helps the attacker. It targets the human, not the machine. Phishing is a fraudulent message, usually an e-mail, that imitates a trusted sender and asks the reader to open an attachment, to follow a link, or to type a password on a false page. When the message is written for one specific person, with real names and real projects, it is called spear phishing. The property harmed first is confidentiality, because a password is disclosed. What monitoring can observe: in the log of the mail service, messages from a domain name that differs by one letter from the name of a real partner; later, a logon to the same account from a country where the company has no employee.

Slide 11

Attack type 3: Malware (1/2): five families

Attack type 3: malware, the short form of malicious software: any program written to harm a system or its user. The families are distinguished by their behaviour. A virus attaches itself to a legitimate file and runs when the user opens that file. A worm copies itself from one computer to another through the network, without any action from a user. A trojan presents itself as a useful program and performs a hidden harmful function. Spyware records what the user does; a keylogger is spyware that records the keys pressed, passwords included.

Slide 12

Attack type 3: Malware (2/2): ransomware

The malware family that causes the largest losses today is ransomware. Ransomware encrypts the files of the victim, which makes them unreadable, and demands a payment for the decryption key. Many groups also copy the files before they encrypt them, and threaten to publish them. One attack then harms availability and confidentiality together. In its National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security names ransomware as the top cybercrime threat to the critical infrastructure of Canada. What monitoring can observe: on a file server, one account that modifies hundreds of files in a few minutes; files that receive a new, unknown extension; and, shortly before, an antivirus alert on a workstation.

Slide 13

Attack type 4: Password attacks

Attack type 4: password attacks. The objective is a valid combination of account name and password. In a brute-force attack, a program tries a very large number of passwords against one account. A dictionary attack is a faster variant that tries only the words of a prepared list of probable passwords. Password spraying reverses the method: the program tries one or two very common passwords against many accounts. Each account receives only one or two attempts, so no account reaches the limit that would lock it. Credential stuffing uses pairs of account names and passwords stolen from another website; it works because many people use the same password in several places. What monitoring can observe: on a Windows server, a series of events with identifier 4625, which means that an account failed to log on. Today's example and today's programs work on exactly this case.

Slide 14

Attack type 5: Denial of service

Attack type 5: denial of service. A DoS (Denial of Service) attack sends a server more requests than it can process, or requests built to make it fail, so that legitimate users no longer receive an answer. When the requests come from thousands of computers at the same time, it is a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack. These computers usually belong to ordinary people; they were infected earlier and are controlled remotely as a group, called a botnet. The property harmed is availability. What monitoring can observe: a traffic volume far above the normal level, a very large number of source addresses, and a response time that rises until the service stops answering.

Slide 15

Attack type 6: On-path attack

Attack type 6: the on-path attack. Its older name is the MITM (Man-in-the-Middle) attack, and you will hear that name in today's video. The attacker places a device between two parties that communicate, so that their traffic passes through this device, where it can be read or modified. Two methods are common on a local network. In ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing, the computer of the attacker sends false address announcements, so that the other computers send their traffic to it. A rogue access point is a wireless access point installed without authorization, which uses the same network name as the office. Confidentiality and integrity are harmed. What monitoring can observe: the same IP (Internet Protocol) address associated with two different hardware addresses, or an access point that uses the office name and is absent from the inventory.

Slide 16

Attack type 7: Injection

Attack type 7: injection, and its best-known form, SQL (Structured Query Language) injection. Many web applications build a database command from the text that a user types in a form. If the application does not verify this text, an attacker can type a fragment of database command in the form field, and the database executes it. The attacker can then read tables that the application was never meant to show, or change their content. What monitoring can observe: in the log of the web server, requests that contain database keywords or unusual punctuation in a field where a name or a number is expected, and a rise in database errors.

Slide 17

Attack type 8: Insider misuse

Attack type 8: insider misuse. The threat actor is a person who already has authorized access: an employee, a former employee whose account was not closed, a contractor. The access is authorized; the purpose is not. Examples: copying the client list before leaving for a competitor, or reading the file of a relative out of curiosity. No technical barrier is broken. This is why prevention cannot stop insider misuse, and why monitoring matters. What monitoring can observe: access to many files outside the normal duties of the person, activity at unusual hours, large copies toward removable media or personal cloud storage.

Slide 18

Two more terms: zero-day attack and supply-chain attack

Two last terms complete the vocabulary. A zero-day attack uses a vulnerability that the software publisher does not know yet, or has not corrected yet: on the day of the attack, no security update exists. A supply-chain attack reaches the target through a supplier: the attacker modifies a software update, or compromises a service provider that the target trusts. In both cases the preventive controls of the organization are intact, and the attack still succeeds. Remember this point. It is the main argument of Lesson 1.4.

Slide 19

Figure 1: attack types and the property each one harms

To summarize Lesson 1.3 from the point of view of monitoring: each attack type harms at least one property, and each attack type leaves observable traces. Figure 1 shows, line by line, the property that each attack type harms. A full circle is the main property harmed; an empty circle is a property that is often harmed as well.

Slide 20

Figure 2: where each attack type can be observed

Each trace is found in a specific data source. Figure 2 places these data sources on the network of our example office: the firewall log, the security log of the server, the workstations, the mail service, and the network switch with the wireless survey. These five points are the first entries of the network map that you will draw in Lab 1.

Real-life example 1. A Friday morning on the file server

Task
Read 15 logon records exported from a file server and decide, for each source address, whether the pattern is a typing mistake, a brute-force attack or password spraying.
Relation to the lecture
Applies the definitions of attack type 4 of Lesson 1.3: brute force is many passwords against one account; password spraying is one or two passwords against many accounts. It also shows what "what monitoring can observe" means in practice: events 4625 and 4624.
Deliverable
One result line per source address: number of failures, number of different accounts, conclusion.
Use in the labs
Lab 1: the two recognition rules enter the monitoring plan as suspicious behaviours to watch on the file server. Lab 2: they become alert rules in the monitoring tool. Lab 3: the result lines are the evidence attached to the anomaly report.

Fictional data only. The organization, the people and the records are invented. The two external addresses belong to blocks reserved for documentation (RFC (Request for Comments) 5737, address blocks reserved for documentation ), so they belong to nobody. Do not replace them with real addresses, and never export or analyse the log of a system that you do not own or are not authorized in writing to work on (Legal Notice, sections 6.1, 6.4, 6.7 and 7.2).

Slide 24

Example 1: a Friday morning on the file server

Example 1 applies Lesson 1.3 to data. The organization is fictional: Trois-Érables Accounting, an office of twelve people in Montréal. Its file server, named TE-FS01, holds the files of the clients. The task: read the logon records of one morning and decide, for each source address, whether the pattern is a typing mistake, a brute-force attack or password spraying.

Slide 26

Example 1: read the log before any program runs

Look at the table before we run any program. Records 2 and 3: one failure, then a success twelve seconds later, same account, same workstation inside the office. This is a person who made a typing mistake. Records 4 to 9: six failures in ten seconds, always on the account administrator, always from the same external address. No person types that fast: it is a program. Many passwords against one account: a brute-force attack. Records 10 to 14: five failures from another external address, one every thirty seconds, each on a different account. One password tried against many accounts: password spraying. Record 15: fifteen minutes later, the same address logs on successfully as j.roy. The attacker has found a valid password.

Slide 27

Program 1: two counters and three rules

The program that follows applies the same reasoning with two counters for each source address: the number of failures, and the number of different accounts. I will run it step by step. Watch the drawing on the right: each record is placed on the line of its source, and the two counters change as the records are read.

Program 1. Recognize a password attack in a logon log

Python
Task of the program
Read the 15 records one by one. For every source address, count the failed logons and the different accounts that were tried. Then apply three rules and print one conclusion per source.
Relation to the lecture
The two counters are the two definitions of Lesson 1.3 turned into numbers: many failures on few accounts is brute force; few failures on many accounts is password spraying. A successful logon after failures from the same source is the sign of a compromised account.
How to use it here
Start runs the program and becomes Pause; after a pause, Resume continues from the same line. Step executes one line. Next record executes all the lines of one log record. Restart returns to the beginning. Select any line of the steps window to return to that moment.
Why Python
The syntax of Python uses plain English words. Python runs the same way on Windows, Linux and macOS, and needs no extra module here. The steps shown were recorded from a real run of this exact program.
Program 1: class03_ex1_recognize_password_attack.py
1# =============================================================================
2# Cyber.SoHo - Educational Hub | 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring | Class 3
3# Example 1 (Lesson 1.3) - Recognize a password attack in a logon log
4# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
5# TASK
6# Read 15 logon records exported from the file server TE-FS01 of the
7# fictional office "Trois-Erables Accounting". For every source address,
8# count the failed logons and the different accounts that were tried.
9# Then decide: typing mistake, brute-force attack, or password spraying.
10#
11# RELATION TO THE LECTURE
12# Lesson 1.3 defines brute force (many passwords against ONE account) and
13# password spraying (one or two passwords against MANY accounts).
14# This script applies these two definitions to monitoring data.
15#
16# USE IN THE LABS
17# Lab 1: the two rules go in the "suspicious behaviours" list of the plan.
18# Lab 2: the two rules become alert rules in the monitoring tool.
19# Lab 3: the printed result is the evidence attached to the anomaly report.
20#
21# SAFE USE
22# Fictional data only. The addresses belong to ranges reserved for
23# documentation and private lab networks. Run this script only inside your
24# Authorized Lab Environment. Requires Python 3.8 or newer, no extra module.
25# (c) 2026 Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov. All rights reserved.
26# Terms: https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
27# =============================================================================
28
29# Store the 15 exported log records as one block of text; each record has four fields separated by commas: time, event identifier, account name, source address.
30LOG = """09:02:11,4624,s.nguyen,192.168.56.24
3109:03:40,4625,m.tremblay,192.168.56.21
3209:03:52,4624,m.tremblay,192.168.56.21
3309:10:01,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3409:10:03,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3509:10:05,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3609:10:07,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3709:10:09,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3809:10:11,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
3909:14:20,4625,a.gagnon,198.51.100.77
4009:14:50,4625,j.roy,198.51.100.77
4109:15:20,4625,l.cote,198.51.100.77
4209:15:50,4625,m.tremblay,198.51.100.77
4309:16:20,4625,s.nguyen,198.51.100.77
4409:31:05,4624,j.roy,198.51.100.77"""
45
46# Give a readable name to the Windows Security event identifier 4625, which means "an account failed to log on".
47FAILED = "4625"
48# Give a readable name to the Windows Security event identifier 4624, which means "an account was successfully logged on".
49SUCCESS = "4624"
50# Teaching threshold: 5 or more failed logons from one source are treated as a brute-force attack (a real threshold comes from the baseline built in Lab 2).
51BRUTE_FORCE_LIMIT = 5
52# Teaching threshold: 4 or more different accounts tried from one source are treated as password spraying.
53SPRAY_LIMIT = 4
54
55# Create an empty dictionary that will hold, for each source address, the number of failed logons seen so far.
56failed_count = {}
57# Create an empty dictionary that will hold, for each source address, the list of different account names that were tried.
58accounts_tried = {}
59# Create an empty dictionary that will hold, for each source address, the account that logged on successfully AFTER that source had failures.
60success_after_fail = {}
61
62# Read the log one record at a time, from the first line to the last, exactly as a monitoring tool does.
63for line in LOG.splitlines():
64 # Cut the record at every comma and store the four parts in four variables with clear names.
65 time_text, event_id, account, source = line.split(",")
66 # Test whether this record is a failed logon, because every password attack produces failed logons.
67 if event_id == FAILED:
68 # Add 1 to the failure counter of this source; get(source, 0) returns 0 when the source is seen for the first time.
69 failed_count[source] = failed_count.get(source, 0) + 1
70 # Test whether this source already has a list of tried accounts.
71 if source not in accounts_tried:
72 # Create the empty list for this new source so that account names can be added to it.
73 accounts_tried[source] = []
74 # Test whether this account name is new for this source, so that each account is counted only once.
75 if account not in accounts_tried[source]:
76 # Add the account name to the list: the length of this list tells how many different accounts were targeted.
77 accounts_tried[source].append(account)
78 # Otherwise, test whether the record is a successful logon coming from a source that already had at least one failure.
79 elif event_id == SUCCESS and failed_count.get(source, 0) > 0:
80 # Remember which account finally logged on from that source: after an attack, this may be a compromised account.
81 success_after_fail[source] = account
82
83# Examine each source that produced at least one failed logon and decide what its pattern means.
84for source in failed_count:
85 # Copy the number of failed logons of this source into a short variable name.
86 fails = failed_count[source]
87 # Count how many different accounts this source tried.
88 targets = len(accounts_tried[source])
89 # Rule 1: many different accounts from one source is the pattern of password spraying.
90 if targets >= SPRAY_LIMIT:
91 # Record the conclusion for this source.
92 verdict = "PASSWORD SPRAYING"
93 # Rule 2: many failures against few accounts from one source is the pattern of a brute-force attack.
94 elif fails >= BRUTE_FORCE_LIMIT:
95 # Record the conclusion for this source.
96 verdict = "BRUTE FORCE"
97 # Rule 3: a small number of failures on one account is the normal pattern of a user who typed the wrong password.
98 else:
99 # Record the conclusion for this source.
100 verdict = "probably a typing mistake"
101 # Test the most serious case: the source is attacking AND one logon from it succeeded.
102 if source in success_after_fail and verdict != "probably a typing mistake":
103 # Extend the conclusion with the name of the account and the action expected from the technician.
104 verdict = verdict + " + LOGON SUCCEEDED for " + success_after_fail[source] + " -> report now"
105 # Print one result line per source: this line is the evidence that the technician copies into the report.
106 print(source, "|", fails, "failed |", targets, "account(s) |", verdict)

    Slide 28
    Program 1: what it counted, and what it printed
    The result is three lines, one for each source that failed at least once, and only the third line asks for an immediate report. These three lines are the deliverable of the example. In Lab 1, the two rules enter your monitoring plan as suspicious behaviours to watch on the file server. In Lab 2, they become alert rules in your monitoring tool. In Lab 3, a result of this kind is the evidence that you attach to your anomaly report.
    
  
    
  
    Step-by-step explanation of Program 1
    
  
      
    
    1. The data. The 15 records are stored in one text variable named LOG. In a real situation the records come from an export of the Security event log of the server. The logic of the program stays the same.
      2. 
    
    2. Four named values. FAILED stands for 4625 and SUCCESS for 4624. BRUTE_FORCE_LIMIT is 5 failures and SPRAY_LIMIT is 4 different accounts. A name is easier to read, and easier to change, than a number repeated in the code.
      3. 
    
    3. Three empty dictionaries. A dictionary stores pairs made of a key and a value. Here the key is always a source address. failed_count stores a number, accounts_tried stores a list of account names, success_after_fail stores one account name.
      4. 
    
    4. The reading loop. for line in LOG.splitlines() takes one record at a time, in order. line.split(",") cuts the record at each comma and gives the four fields.
      5. 
    
    5. A failed logon. The program adds 1 to the counter of the source. It adds the account name to the list of that source only if the name is not in the list yet. The length of the list is therefore the number of different accounts.
      6. 
    
    6. A successful logon. The program checks whether the same source failed before. If yes, it remembers the account. A success that follows failures from the same source is the most serious sign in this log.
      7. 
    
    7. The three rules, in a fixed order. 4 different accounts or more: password spraying. If not, 5 failures or more: brute force. If not: a typing mistake. The order matters, because the spraying source also has 5 failures and must not be classified as brute force.
      8. 
    
    8. The output. One line per source. Workstation 192.168.56.24 does not appear: it never failed, and the program reports only the sources that failed at least once. The third line ends with "report now", because a logon succeeded from a source that was attacking.
      9. 
  
    
  
    Limits of this teaching program. The two limits, 5 and 4, are teaching values. Real thresholds come from the baseline of normal activity that you will build in Lab 2. The program ignores time: six failures in ten seconds and six failures in six months count the same. Program 2 corrects this with a time window.

    1.4
    Basic cyber defense concepts: prevention, detection, response
    ReadingExampleProgramFiguresVideosCardsCheck
    Lesson 1.4 is folded. Select “Unfold lesson” to open it again.
    

    
  
    Reading
    
  
    
    
    Slide 30
    Lesson 1.4
Basic cyber defense concepts
    
    
    Three functions, classified by the moment at which they act
    

    Slide 31
    Security controls act at three moments
    Lesson 1.4: basic cyber defense concepts. Cyber defense is the set of measures that an organization uses to protect its information and its systems against cyberattacks. A single measure is called a security control. Controls are classified by the moment at which they act. A preventive control acts before the attack succeeds, and tries to make it fail. A detective control acts during the attack or shortly after it, and makes it visible. A corrective control acts after the incident is confirmed: it limits the damage and returns the systems to normal operation. These three moments give the three functions of cyber defense: prevention, detection and response.
    

    Slide 32
    Prevention: seven controls you meet most often
    Prevention first. Here are the preventive controls that you will meet most often, each with the attack that it addresses. Security updates, also called patches, correct known vulnerabilities before they are used. MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) asks for a second proof of identity, for example a code generated on a telephone, so that a stolen password alone is not sufficient. An account lockout policy blocks an account after a fixed number of failed logons, and stops a brute-force attack. A firewall allows only the network connections that a rule authorizes. The principle of least privilege gives each account only the rights needed for the work of its owner; this limits what a compromised account, or a dishonest insider, can reach. Backups kept offline make recovery possible after ransomware. Awareness training teaches employees to recognize phishing.
    

    Slide 33
    Why prevention is never sufficient
    Prevention is necessary, and it is never sufficient. There are four reasons. One: a zero-day attack uses a vulnerability for which no update exists. Two: people make errors, and one employee in a hundred who types a password on a false page is enough. Three: an insider already holds authorized access. Four: every organization has limited money and limited staff, so some systems are always less protected than others. A professional defender therefore assumes that some attacks will pass the preventive controls, and prepares to see them and to act. Seeing them is detection. It is the subject of this course.
    
  
    
  
    
    
    Detection: data sources, a baseline and rules
    

    Slide 34
    Detection needs three things
    Detection is the identification, as early as possible, of events that may indicate an attack. Detection needs three things. First, data sources: the event logs of servers and workstations, the logs of the firewall and of other network equipment, captured network traffic, and the alerts of security software. Second, a baseline: a recorded description of the normal activity of the network, for example the number of failed logons on a normal morning. Without a baseline, nobody can say that an activity is abnormal. You will build a baseline in Lab 2. Third, detection rules. A rule with a threshold raises an alert when a count passes a limit within a period of time: for example, five failed logons from one source in ten minutes. A rule with a signature raises an alert when the data matches the known pattern of a specific attack.
    

    Slide 35
    Tools that apply the rules
    Three families of tools apply these rules. An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) analyses network traffic or the activity of a computer, and raises alerts. An IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) does the same and can also block the traffic, which makes it a preventive control as well. A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform collects the logs of many systems in one place, relates events from different sources to each other, and raises alerts. In a large organization, the people who read these alerts work in a SOC (Security Operations Centre).
    

    Slide 36
    Event, alert, incident
    Three words must be used with precision. An event is any recorded occurrence: a logon, a file opened. An alert is a notification produced by a rule. An incident is an event, or a group of events, that a person has analysed and confirmed as harmful. Thousands of events produce tens of alerts, and a few alerts become incidents.
    

    Slide 37
    False positive, false negative and tuning
    No rule is perfect. A false positive is an alert raised for a legitimate activity: the accountant who forgot her password on a Monday morning. A false negative is a real attack for which no alert was raised. If a threshold is too low, the technicians receive so many false positives that they stop reading the alerts. If it is too high, attacks pass without an alert. Adjusting the rules to reduce both errors is called tuning, and it is the subject of Topic 6. The speed of detection is measured by the MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): the average time between the start of an attack and its detection.
    
  
    
  
    
    
    Response: five steps, under supervision
    

    Slide 38
    Response: five steps
    Response is the set of actions taken when an incident is confirmed. The reference document is the incident response guide of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), publication SP (Special Publication) 800-61, revised in 2025. For this course, remember five steps. Preparation: before any incident, the organization writes a plan, names the people responsible and keeps their contact information up to date. Analysis: the technician verifies the alert, and determines what happened and which systems are affected. Containment: limit the damage, for example by disabling a compromised account or by isolating an infected workstation from the network. Eradication and recovery: remove the cause, restore the data from backups, return to normal operation. Lessons learned: record what happened and improve the controls. The speed of response is measured by the MTTR (Mean Time to Respond), from the detection to the end of the recovery.
    

    Slide 39
    Your part in the response: under supervision
    What is your part in the response? The competency of this course states that you work under supervision. In practice, the monitoring technician detects, analyses, documents and reports. The technician does not decide alone to block an address, to disable an account or to shut down a server on a production network. A containment action changes the system and can interrupt the work of legitimate users. It requires the approval of the person responsible for that system. Section 7.4 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice gives the same rule for your laboratory work. Your most valuable product is a clear incident note: what was observed, when, on which system, from which source, and what you recommend.
    

    Slide 40
    In Québec: Law 25 and the confidentiality incident
    In Québec, response also has a legal part. Under the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, as amended by Law 25, an incident that involves personal information is a confidentiality incident. The organization must record it in a register. If the incident presents a risk of serious injury, the organization must notify the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) and the persons concerned. This decision belongs to the person responsible for the protection of personal information, not to the technician. But this person can decide correctly only if your incident note is accurate and arrives quickly.
    

    Slide 41
    Defense in depth
    Two last ideas. Defense in depth means that several independent controls are placed one after the other, so that the failure of one control does not give access to the information. In today's second example, two controls react differently to the same log: the account lockout, a preventive control, stops one attack and never reacts to the other; the detection rule sees both.
    

    Slide 42
    Figure 3: the three functions work as a cycle
    Finally, the reference frameworks contain the same three functions under other names. The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 has six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Protect corresponds to prevention, Detect to detection, Respond and Recover to response. Govern and Identify are the foundation: know the rules, and know the network. That foundation is Topic 2 and Lab 1.
    
    
    Sources: Incident response project of the National Institute of Standards and Technology  for the response steps; Cybersecurity Framework 2.0  for the six functions; Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector  and the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec  for the duties that follow a confidentiality incident; Ransomware playbook  of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security as a complete worked case of prevention, detection and response.
    
  
    

    


    
  
    Real-life example 2. Which defense function reacted?
    
  
    
    
    Task
    Process the same 15 logon records in time order, as a monitoring tool receives them, and observe three controls: a preventive control (account lockout), a detective control (alert rule with a time window) and the start of a response (incident note with recommended actions).
    
    
    Relation to the lecture
    Shows with data why prevention alone is not sufficient: the lockout stops the brute-force attack and never reacts to the password spraying. Shows what detection needs: a rule, a threshold, a time window, and a person who reads the alert. Shows the role of the technician in the response: document, report and recommend.
    
    
    Deliverable
    An incident note with the times of the lockout and of the two alerts, the time to detect, the high-priority line, and four recommended actions for the supervisor.
    
    
    Use in the labs
    Lab 1: decide which asset needs which control, and write it in the monitoring plan. Lab 2: the alert rule of this example is the first alert that you configure. Lab 3: the incident note is the format of your anomaly report.
    
  
    
  
    The program blocks nothing and changes nothing. It prints a recommendation. On a real system, every containment action needs the written approval of the owner of the system, a change window and a tested rollback (Legal Notice, section 7.4). Measures that reach out to another system, or act against it, are prohibited in every course of the program. If you ever discover a real incident, stop, document what you saw and report it (section 6.8).
    
  
    

    Slide 43
    Example 2: which defense function reacted?
    Example 2 uses the same fifteen records and asks the question of Lesson 1.4: which defense function reacts to which attack? The office has one preventive control on its server: an account is locked after five failed logons in a row. We add one detective control: an alert when one source address produces five failed logons within ten minutes. And we add the start of a response: the program writes an incident note.
    

    Slide 44
    Program 2 at 09:10:09: both controls react to the brute-force attack
    Run the program and watch the three panels. At 09:10:09, the fifth failure on the account administrator arrives. The prevention panel shows the account locked, and the detection panel raises an alert in the same second. Both controls worked.
    

    Slide 45
    Program 2 at 09:16:20: only detection sees the password spraying
    Now the spraying. Each account receives one failure only. The prevention panel never reaches five for any account: the lockout does not react at all. The detection panel counts by source, not by account, and raises its alert at 09:16:20, two minutes after the first attempt.
    

    Slide 46
    Program 2 at 09:31:05: the attacker logs on
    The successful logon of the attacker arrives at 09:31:05. The response panel receives a high-priority line, because this logon comes from a source that is already under alert. The attacker has probably found a valid password.
    

    Slide 47
    Figure 4: detection gave the office 14 minutes 45 seconds
    Between the alert and that logon there are fourteen minutes and forty-five seconds. This is the time that detection gave to the office. If somebody reads the alert and obtains the approval to block the source during this time, no account is compromised. If nobody reads it, detection had no effect. Figure 4 shows this timeline.
    

    Slide 48
    Program 2: the incident note and the recommended response
    Note also the last lines of the output: the program recommends actions and changes nothing. The approval belongs to the supervisor.
    
  
    

    


    
  
    Program 2. Prevention, detection and response on one log
    Python
    
  
    
    
    Task of the program
    For each record, in time order: update the number of failed logons in a row of the account and lock the account at 5 (prevention); update the failed logons of the source during the last 10 minutes and raise an alert at 5 (detection); write every action in an incident note and, at the end, print the note with four recommended actions (response).
    
    
    Relation to the lecture
    Each variable of the program belongs to one of the three functions of Lesson 1.4, and the three panels of the drawing show them side by side. The time to detect printed in the note is one measurement of the kind that the MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) averages.
    
    
    How to use it here
    Same buttons as Program 1. Use Next record and stop at record 8, at record 14 and at record 15: compare the three panels each time.
    
  
    

    Program 2: class03_ex2_prevent_detect_respond.py
    1# =============================================================================
    

    2# Cyber.SoHo - Educational Hub | 420-1C1-DW Preventative Monitoring | Class 3
    

    3# Example 2 (Lesson 1.4) - Prevention, detection and response on one log
    

    4# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
    

    5# TASK
    

    6#   Process the same 15 logon records in time order, as a monitoring tool
    

    7#   does, and apply three controls:
    

    8#     PREVENTION - lock an account after 5 failed logons in a row;
    

    9#     DETECTION  - raise an alert at 5 failed logons from one source address
    

    10#                  within 10 minutes;
    

    11#     RESPONSE   - write the incident note and the recommended actions.
    

    12#
    

    13# RELATION TO THE LECTURE
    

    14#   Lesson 1.4 explains that prevention alone is not sufficient. In this log
    

    15#   the account lockout stops the brute-force attack, but it never acts
    

    16#   against password spraying. Only the detection rule notices the spraying.
    

    17#
    

    18# USE IN THE LABS
    

    19#   Lab 1: decide which asset needs which control (monitoring plan).
    

    20#   Lab 2: the detection rule below is the first alert you will configure.
    

    21#   Lab 3: the incident note printed at the end is the format of your report.
    

    22#
    

    23# SAFE USE
    

    24#   This script blocks nothing and changes nothing: it only prints a
    

    25#   recommendation. On a real system, every containment action needs the
    

    26#   written approval of the owner of the system (Legal Notice, section 7.4).
    

    27#   Fictional data only. Run inside your Authorized Lab Environment.
    

    28#   Requires Python 3.8 or newer, no extra module.
    

    29#   (c) 2026 Cyber.SoHo / Asen Grozdanov. All rights reserved.
    

    30#   Terms: https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
    

    31# =============================================================================
    

    32 
    

    33# Import two tools from the standard "datetime" module: datetime reads a clock time from text, timedelta represents a duration.
    

    34from datetime import datetime, timedelta
    

    35 
    

    36# Store the same 15 exported log records as in Example 1: time, event identifier, account name, source address.
    

    37LOG = """09:02:11,4624,s.nguyen,192.168.56.24
    

    3809:03:40,4625,m.tremblay,192.168.56.21
    

    3909:03:52,4624,m.tremblay,192.168.56.21
    

    4009:10:01,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4109:10:03,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4209:10:05,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4309:10:07,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4409:10:09,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4509:10:11,4625,administrator,203.0.113.45
    

    4609:14:20,4625,a.gagnon,198.51.100.77
    

    4709:14:50,4625,j.roy,198.51.100.77
    

    4809:15:20,4625,l.cote,198.51.100.77
    

    4909:15:50,4625,m.tremblay,198.51.100.77
    

    5009:16:20,4625,s.nguyen,198.51.100.77
    

    5109:31:05,4624,j.roy,198.51.100.77"""
    

    52 
    

    53# PREVENTION setting: an account is locked when it reaches 5 failed logons in a row (simplified model of an account lockout policy).
    

    54LOCKOUT_LIMIT = 5
    

    55# DETECTION setting: an alert is raised when one source address reaches 5 failed logons inside the time window.
    

    56ALERT_THRESHOLD = 5
    

    57# DETECTION setting: the time window is 10 minutes; older failures are no longer counted.
    

    58WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=10)
    

    59 
    

    60# Create an empty dictionary: for each account, the number of failed logons in a row (used by the prevention control).
    

    61fails_in_a_row = {}
    

    62# Create an empty list: the accounts that the prevention control has locked.
    

    63locked_accounts = []
    

    64# Create an empty dictionary: for each source address, the times of its failed logons that are still inside the window (used by the detection control).
    

    65recent_fail_times = {}
    

    66# Create an empty dictionary: for each source address, the time of its very first failed logon (used to measure the time to detect).
    

    67first_fail_time = {}
    

    68# Create an empty list: the source addresses that have already raised an alert, so that each source alerts only once.
    

    69alerted_sources = []
    

    70# Create an empty list: the lines of the incident note, written as things happen (used by the response function).
    

    71incident_notes = []
    

    72 
    

    73# Read the log one record at a time, in time order, exactly as a monitoring tool receives events.
    

    74for line in LOG.splitlines():
    

    75    # Cut the record at every comma and store the four parts in four variables with clear names.
    

    76    time_text, event_id, account, source = line.split(",")
    

    77    # Convert the text "09:10:01" into a real clock time, so that the program can subtract two times.
    

    78    now = datetime.strptime(time_text, "%H:%M:%S")
    

    79    # Test whether this record is a failed logon (event identifier 4625).
    

    80    if event_id == "4625":
    

    81        # PREVENTION: add 1 to the number of failed logons in a row for this account.
    

    82        fails_in_a_row[account] = fails_in_a_row.get(account, 0) + 1
    

    83        # PREVENTION: test whether the account has just reached the lockout limit.
    

    84        if fails_in_a_row[account] == LOCKOUT_LIMIT:
    

    85            # PREVENTION: lock the account, which stops any further password guessing against it.
    

    86            locked_accounts.append(account)
    

    87            # RESPONSE: write down what the preventive control did, with the time, for the incident note.
    

    88            incident_notes.append(time_text + " PREVENTION account " + account + " locked after 5 failed logons in a row")
    

    89        # DETECTION: test whether this is the first failed logon ever seen from this source.
    

    90        if source not in first_fail_time:
    

    91            # DETECTION: remember when this source started to fail; this is the start time used to measure the time to detect.
    

    92            first_fail_time[source] = now
    

    93        # DETECTION: build the list of earlier failure times of this source that are 10 minutes old or less; older ones are dropped.
    

    94        times = [t for t in recent_fail_times.get(source, []) if now - t <= WINDOW]
    

    95        # DETECTION: add the time of the current failed logon to that list.
    

    96        times.append(now)
    

    97        # DETECTION: store the updated list back in the dictionary under this source address.
    

    98        recent_fail_times[source] = times
    

    99        # DETECTION: test the alert rule - threshold reached inside the window, and no alert raised yet for this source.
    

    100        if len(times) >= ALERT_THRESHOLD and source not in alerted_sources:
    

    101            # DETECTION: remember that this source has raised an alert, so that the same alert is not repeated at every new failure.
    

    102            alerted_sources.append(source)
    

    103            # DETECTION: measure the time to detect, from the first failed logon of this source to this alert.
    

    104            delay = now - first_fail_time[source]
    

    105            # RESPONSE: write the alert in the incident note with the facts a supervisor needs: time, count, source, time to detect.
    

    106            incident_notes.append(time_text + " DETECTION ALERT " + str(len(times)) + " failed logons from " + source + " in 10 min, detected after " + str(delay))
    

    107    # Otherwise the record is a successful logon (event identifier 4624).
    

    108    else:
    

    109        # PREVENTION: a successful logon sets the number of failed logons in a row of this account back to 0.
    

    110        fails_in_a_row[account] = 0
    

    111        # RESPONSE: test the most serious case - a successful logon that comes from a source already under alert.
    

    112        if source in alerted_sources:
    

    113            # RESPONSE: write a high-priority line, because the attacker has probably found a valid password.
    

    114            incident_notes.append(time_text + " RESPONSE HIGH PRIORITY " + account + " logged on from alerted source " + source)
    

    115 
    

    116# Print the title of the incident note with the name of the server and the date of the log.
    

    117print("INCIDENT NOTE - file server TE-FS01 - 2026-09-18 (fictional data)")
    

    118# Go through the incident note lines in the order in which they were written.
    

    119for note in incident_notes:
    

    120    # Print one line of the incident note.
    

    121    print(note)
    

    122# Print the heading of the recommendation and state clearly that a person with authority must approve it.
    

    123print("RECOMMENDED RESPONSE - to be approved by the supervisor before any change:")
    

    124# Print containment: limit the damage first.
    

    125print("1. Contain: disable account j.roy, block 198.51.100.77 and 203.0.113.45 on firewall TE-FW01")
    

    126# Print eradication and recovery: remove the cause and return to normal.
    

    127print("2. Recover: reset the password of j.roy, review what the account opened after 09:31:05, unlock administrator")
    

    128# Print reporting: inform the people concerned, including the person responsible for personal information.
    

    129print("3. Report: send this note to the supervisor; the privacy officer evaluates the Law 25 obligations")
    

    130# Print improvement: correct the weakness that this incident revealed.
    

    131print("4. Improve: require multi-factor authentication for remote logon and keep this alert rule active")

      Step-by-step explanation of Program 2
      
  
        
    
      1. Working with time. The first line imports datetime, which represents a clock time, and timedelta, which represents a duration. The program needs them to subtract one time from another.
        2. 
    
      2. Three settings. LOCKOUT_LIMIT = 5 belongs to prevention. ALERT_THRESHOLD = 5 and WINDOW = timedelta(minutes=10) belong to detection.
        3. 
    
      3. Six empty containers, each owned by one function. fails_in_a_row and locked_accounts: prevention. recent_fail_times, first_fail_time and alerted_sources: detection. incident_notes: response.
        4. 
    
      4. The loop and the clock. The records are read in time order. datetime.strptime(time_text, "%H:%M:%S") converts the text 09:10:01 into a time value.
        5. 
    
      5. Prevention counts per account. Each failure adds 1 to the failures in a row of the account. At exactly 5, the account enters locked_accounts and a line is written in the note. A successful logon sets the counter of that account back to 0.
        6. 
    
      6. Detection counts per source address, inside a time window. The line that contains for t in builds a new list and keeps only the failure times that are 10 minutes old or less. Then the current time is added.
        7. 
    
      7. The alert. When the list reaches 5 and the source has not raised an alert yet, the program records the source, measures the time to detect with now - first_fail_time[source], and writes the alert in the note.
        8. 
    
      8. From detection to response. A successful logon from a source that is already under alert produces a high-priority line. It is the most important line of the note.
        9. 
    
      9. The note and the recommendation. The program prints the note, then four actions in the order of the response steps: contain, recover, report, improve. It executes none of them. A person with authority approves.
        10. 
  
      
  
      Limits of this teaching program. The lockout is simplified: a real Windows lockout policy also has a period after which the counter returns to zero and a duration of the lockout, and a locked account refuses every further logon. The log contains times without dates. The thresholds are teaching values; real ones come from the baseline of Lab 2.

      Slide 50
      Table 2: control map (2/2)
      
  
      Table 2. Control map: prevention, detection and response for each attack type
      Attack typePrevention: preventive controlsDetection: what to raise an alert onResponse: first actions, with the approval of the supervisor
      ReconnaissanceFirewall rules that close every port that is not needed; no unnecessary service reachable from the Internet.One source that tries many ports or addresses in a short time.Record the source and the time; verify that nothing answered; recommend blocking the source.
      PhishingAwareness training; mail filtering; multi-factor authentication, so that a stolen password is not sufficient.Messages from look-alike domain names; logon from an unusual place after such a message.Reset the password of the account; remove the message from the other mailboxes; inform the employees.
      MalwareSecurity updates; antivirus; no administrator rights for daily work.Antivirus alert; unknown process; connection toward an unknown external address.Isolate the workstation from the network; keep the evidence; reinstall or clean according to the plan.
      RansomwareOffline backups; least privilege on file shares; security updates.Mass modification of files by one account; new unknown file extensions.Isolate the affected systems at once; restore from backups; evaluate the Law 25 duties if personal information is involved.
      Brute force and dictionary attacksAccount lockout policy; long passwords; multi-factor authentication.Five or more failed logons on one account, or from one source, within ten minutes.Verify the lockout; record the source; recommend blocking it on the firewall.
      Password spraying and credential stuffingMulti-factor authentication; refusal of very common passwords; no reuse of passwords.Failed logons on many different accounts from one source; a success after these failures.Disable the compromised account; reset its password; review what the account opened; recommend blocking the source.
      Denial of serviceProtection service of the Internet provider; capacity planning; rate limits.Traffic far above the baseline; response time of the service that rises.Inform the Internet provider; apply the filtering that it offers; inform the users.
      On-path attackEncrypted protocols; protection functions of the network switch; inventory of authorized access points.One address with two hardware addresses; unknown access point with the office name.Locate and disconnect the device; reset the passwords that may have been read.
      Injection in a databaseVerification of every input by the application; least privilege for the database account; security updates.Database keywords in form fields; rise in database errors.Inform the owner of the application; restrict the access; review which tables were read.
      Insider misuseLeast privilege; separation of duties; closing of accounts on the day of departure.Access outside normal duties or hours; large copies of files.Preserve the logs; report to the supervisor only; the organization decides the follow-up.
      The actions of the last column are recommendations that the technician writes in the incident note. Each one needs the approval of the person responsible for the system (Legal Notice, section 7.4).

      Slide 55
      To close: three functions, one role for you
      Tomorrow, in Class 4, we finish Topic 1 with the difference between a security issue and a performance issue, and you write Quiz 1. It counts for 5 percent and covers all the material presented up to tomorrow, today's two lessons included. The flash cards and the knowledge checks of this page are practice material. They are not graded, and they are not the quiz.
      

      To close. An attack harms confidentiality, integrity or availability, and it leaves traces. Prevention reduces the number of attacks that succeed. Detection makes the others visible. Response limits their effect. You are being trained for the second function, and you need to understand the two others to do it well.
